claim: RecA forms a helical filament on single stranded DNA during homologous recombination
source: During homologous recombination, RecA forms a helical filament on a single stranded (ss) DNA that searches for a homologous double stranded (ds) DNA and catalyzes the exchange of complementary base pairs to form a new heteroduplex.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known function of RecA

claim: RecA filament diffuses along dsDNA track during homology search
source: We present evidence in support of the 'sliding model' wherein a RecA filament diffuses along a dsDNA track.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Homology can be detected during RecA filament sliding
source: We further show that homology can be detected during sliding.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data in Figure 4

claim: RecA filament sliding occurs with a diffusion coefficient of approximately 8000 bp²/s
source: Sliding occurs with a diffusion coefficient of approximately 8000 bp2/s allowing the filament to sample several hundred base pairs before dissociation.
evidence: This value is derived from Monte Carlo simulations fitted to experimental cross-correlation data

claim: RecA filament can sample several hundred base pairs before dissociation
source: Sliding occurs with a diffusion coefficient of approximately 8000 bp2/s allowing the filament to sample several hundred base pairs before dissociation.
evidence: This is calculated from the diffusion coefficient and lifetime measurements

claim: Sliding can accelerate homology search by as much as 200 fold
source: Modeling suggests that sliding can accelerate homology search by as much as 200 fold.
evidence: This is derived from theoretical modeling based on experimental parameters

claim: Homology recognition can occur for as few as 6 nt of complementary base pairs
source: Homology recognition can occur for as few as 6 nt of complementary basepairs with the recognition efficiency increasing for higher complementarity.
evidence: This is demonstrated experimentally in Figure 4 with different homology lengths

claim: Recognition efficiency increases with higher complementarity
source: Homology recognition can occur for as few as 6 nt of complementary basepairs with the recognition efficiency increasing for higher complementarity.
evidence: This is shown by comparing recognition efficiencies for 6 nt vs 7 nt homology sites

claim: This is the first example of a DNA bound multi-protein complex which can slide along another DNA to facilitate target search
source: Our data represents the first example of a DNA bound multi-protein complex which can slide along another DNA to facilitate target search.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the context of existing literature

claim: Homologous recombination is one of the pathways involved in double strand break repair
source: Homologous recombination is one of the pathways involved in double strand break repair (Cox et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation

claim: RecA in E. coli catalyzes strand exchange during homologous recombination
source: An important step in homologous recombination is the reciprocal exchange of basepairs between complementary DNA molecules during a reaction called strand exchange, which is catalyzed by RecA in E. coli.
evidence: This is established knowledge about RecA function

claim: Rad51 and Dmc1 in eukaryotes are homologs of RecA that carry out similar functions
source: Homologs of RecA, Rad51 and Dmc1 in eukaryotes and RadA in archaea, carry out similar functions during DNA repair underscoring the central role of proteins catalyzing strand exchange across all forms of life (Bianco et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation

claim: RadA in archaea is a homolog of RecA that carries out similar functions
source: Homologs of RecA, Rad51 and Dmc1 in eukaryotes and RadA in archaea, carry out similar functions during DNA repair underscoring the central role of proteins catalyzing strand exchange across all forms of life (Bianco et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation

claim: RecA assembles on ssDNA with a stoichiometry of 3 nt per monomer
source: Pre-synapsis involves the assembly of RecA monomers on single stranded (ss) DNA in the presence of ATP with a stoichiometry of 3 nt per monomer (Di Capua et al., 1982; Dombroski et al., 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: RecA filament stretches ssDNA to 1.5 times the length of B-form DNA
source: RecA forms a filament which stretches the ssDNA to a length of 1.5 times the length of B-form DNA (Stasiak et al., 1981; Dunn et al., 1982; Stasiak and Egelman, 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations

claim: The strand exchange reaction involves three steps: pre-synapsis, synapsis, and heteroduplex extension via branch migration
source: The strand exchange reaction involves three steps: (1) pre-synapsis, (2) synapsis, and (3) heteroduplex extension via branch migration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the strand exchange mechanism

claim: Homology search is the first step in synapsis and is the most mysterious aspect of the strand exchange reaction
source: Homology search is the first step in synapsis and is arguably the most mysterious aspect of the strand exchange reaction (Barzel and Kupiec, 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the field supported by citation

claim: The multivalent nature of RecA filament enables sustained contact with dsDNA while allowing frequent dissociation events
source: The multivalent nature of the RecA filament enables it to sustain contact with a long dsDNA while allowing for frequent dissociation events that permits rapid sampling of different segments of the DNA, thus facilitating homology search (Forget and Kowalczykowski, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation

claim: Mechanical manipulation experiments identified structural intermediates that facilitate homology recognition
source: Experiments involving the mechanical manipulation of the incoming dsDNA upon binding to the RecA filament identified structural intermediates which facilitate homology recognition and provided insight into mechanisms by which RecA can discriminate between homologous and non-homologous DNA sequences (Danilowicz et al., 2012; De Vlaminck et al., 2012; Peacock-Villada et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from prior studies supported by citations

claim: Random 3D collision between RecA filament and dsDNA is unlikely to result in precise alignment of matching sequences
source: However, random 3D collision between a RecA filament and the dsDNA even when aided by intersegmental transfer is unlikely to result in precise alignment of matching sequences.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the limitations of 3D collision-based search

claim: RecA filament sliding over ten to hundreds of bp would significantly accelerate the search for homology
source: For this reason, RecA filament sliding on dsDNA, even over a short distance range of ten to hundreds of bp would significantly accelerate the search for homology.
evidence: This is a logical inference that motivates the study

claim: Many proteins are known to diffuse along DNA via 1D sliding
source: Although many proteins are now known to diffuse along the DNA via 1D sliding (Blainey et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Gorman et al., 2007; Bonnet et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Roy et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011) RecA filament diffusion on DNA has not been observed before and in fact an early study ruled out a role for long range (approximately several kb) 1D sliding during homology search (Adzuma, 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations

claim: RecA filament diffusion on DNA has not been observed before this study
source: Although many proteins are now known to diffuse along the DNA via 1D sliding (Blainey et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Gorman et al., 2007; Bonnet et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Roy et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011) RecA filament diffusion on DNA has not been observed before and in fact an early study ruled out a role for long range (approximately several kb) 1D sliding during homology search (Adzuma, 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature supported by citation

claim: An early study ruled out a role for long range (several kb) 1D sliding during homology search
source: Although many proteins are now known to diffuse along the DNA via 1D sliding (Blainey et al., 2006; Wang et al., 2006; Gorman et al., 2007; Bonnet et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2008; Roy et al., 2009; Zhou et al., 2011) RecA filament diffusion on DNA has not been observed before and in fact an early study ruled out a role for long range (approximately several kb) 1D sliding during homology search (Adzuma, 1998).
evidence: This is prior knowledge supported by citation

claim: For short (<80 bp) homologous dsDNA substrates, homology search is completed rapidly (within 30 ms) once dsDNA encounters a RecA filament
source: For short (<80 bp) homologous dsDNA substrates, homology search is completed rapidly (within 30 ms) once the dsDNA encounters a RecA filament (Ragunathan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from the authors' previous work supported by citation

claim: Non-homologous dsDNA was used to avoid stable product formation and monitor RecA filament during homology search
source: Therefore, we used a non-homologous dsDNA to avoid stable product formation and monitor RecA filament in the act of homology search.
evidence: This is an experimental design choice explained in the text

claim: RecA filaments formed with ATPγS are stable and can carry out strand exchange reaction with homologous dsDNA
source: RecA filaments formed under these conditions are stable and can carry out the strand exchange reaction with a homologous dsDNA (Ragunathan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is prior knowledge from the authors' previous work supported by citation

claim: Docking of non-homologous dsDNA to RecA filament results in large and rapid fluctuations in FRET
source: After docking, we observed large and rapid fluctuations in FRET detected as anti-correlated changes of donor and acceptor intensities.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation shown in Figure 1B

claim: FRET fluctuations are indicative of extensive distance changes between donor on dsDNA and acceptor on RecA/ssDNA filament
source: The FRET fluctuations are indicative of extensive distance changes between the donor on the dsDNA and the acceptor on the RecA/ssDNA filament.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FRET data based on FRET principles

claim: The lifetime of non-homologous dsDNA binding events is exponentially distributed with an average lifetime of 3.5 s
source: The lifetime of the binding events is exponentially distributed with an average lifetime of 3.5 s (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is derived from experimental data shown in Figure 1C

claim: Filaments formed with ATP displayed similar FRET fluctuations and comparable dissociation times to those formed with ATPγS
source: Filaments formed with ATP displayed similar FRET fluctuations upon docking of non-homologous dsDNA and exhibit comparable dissociation times (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The FRET fluctuations do not require ATP hydrolysis
source: Hence, the fluctuations observed here do not require ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ATPγS (non-hydrolyzable) produces similar fluctuations

claim: Different lengths of ssDNA tail (50 or 99 nt) did not significantly change the lifetime of the encounter complex
source: Using different lengths for the ssDNA tail (Lfilament = 50 or 99 nt) did not significantly change the lifetime of the encounter complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Increasing dsDNA length increased the lifetime of the encounter complex
source: In contrast, increasing dsDNA length increased the lifetime presumably due to a larger number of contacts between the dsDNA and the RecA filament (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B with interpretation

claim: The lifetime of the transient encounter complex decreased with increasing magnesium or sodium concentrations
source: Rapid FRET fluctuations persisted under all the solution conditions tested while the lifetime of the complex decreased with increasing magnesium or sodium concentrations suggesting that the interaction is electrostatic in nature and can be weakened by increased screening (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1D-F

claim: The interaction between RecA filament and dsDNA is electrostatic in nature
source: Rapid FRET fluctuations persisted under all the solution conditions tested while the lifetime of the complex decreased with increasing magnesium or sodium concentrations suggesting that the interaction is electrostatic in nature and can be weakened by increased screening (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is inferred from the salt dependence of the interaction lifetime

claim: Eliminating negative charge from RecA C-terminus by deletion of acidic residues resulted in increased lifetime of dsDNA bound to RecA filament
source: Indeed, eliminating negative charge from the RecA C-terminus (Lusetti et al., 2003) by deletion of acidic residues resulted in an increased lifetime of dsDNA bound to the RecA filament (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: Limited unwinding of dsDNA by RecA filament could result in separation of duplex ends
source: The first involves limited unwinding of the dsDNA (Bianchi et al., 1985) by the RecA filament resulting in separation of the duplex ends.
evidence: This is a hypothesis considered based on prior knowledge

claim: Separation of duplex ends is not the source of FRET fluctuations
source: When the dsDNA docks to an unlabeled RecA filament immobilized on the surface, we observed stable high FRET (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) suggesting that separation of the duplex ends is not the source of FRET fluctuations described in Figure 1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Shorter RecA filaments (21 nt) exhibited more rapid FRET changes and smaller amplitudes compared to longer filaments (99 nt)
source: Shorter RecA filaments (Lfilament = 21 nt) exhibited more rapid FRET changes and of smaller amplitudes (Figure 2A) compared to longer filaments (Lfilament = 99 nt) which showed larger and slower changes in FRET (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2A and 2B

claim: The average cross correlation time increased with increasing filament lengths
source: The average cross correlation time increased with increasing filament lengths (Figure 2C), supporting the 1D sliding model.
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2C

claim: The histogram of FRET efficiencies shifted towards lower FRET values for increasing filament lengths
source: Furthermore, the histogram of FRET efficiencies (E) shifted towards lower FRET values for increasing filament lengths (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2D

claim: The RecA filament was treated as a rigid rod in simulations due to its large persistence length of about 800 nm
source: Given its large persistence length of about 800 nm (Hegner et al., 1999), we treated the RecA filament as a rigid rod.
evidence: This is a modeling assumption based on prior knowledge

claim: The diffusion constant for 1D sliding of dsDNA relative to RecA filament is approximately 0.9 × 10⁻³ μm²/s or 7700 bp²/s
source: By comparing the simulation results with the experimental data we estimated the diffusion constant Dslide for 1D sliding of dsDNA relative to the RecA filament to be approximately 0.9 × 10−3 μm2/s or 7700 bp2/s.
evidence: This is derived from Monte Carlo simulations fitted to experimental data

claim: The time scale of sliding does not change as a function of sodium or magnesium ion concentrations
source: Additionally the time scale of sliding (as measured by the cross correlation time) does not change as a function of sodium or magnesium ion concentrations in solution while the sliding time scale increases twofold when ATPγS is replaced by ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B

claim: The sliding time scale increases twofold when ATPγS is replaced by ATP
source: Additionally the time scale of sliding (as measured by the cross correlation time) does not change as a function of sodium or magnesium ion concentrations in solution while the sliding time scale increases twofold when ATPγS is replaced by ATP (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A–B).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B

claim: The two acceptors Cy5 and Cy7 are separated by 33 nt in the three-color FRET assay
source: Here, the immobilized RecA filament is labeled with two different acceptor fluorophores, Cy5 at the ssDNA/dsDNA junction and Cy7 in the middle of the ssDNA embedded within the RecA filament (Figure 3A). The two acceptors are separated by 33 nt, which upon RecA binding results in a large separation and negligible FRET between them (Joo et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the experimental design and shown in Figure 3A

claim: The sliding model predicts anticorrelated changes between ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7
source: The sliding model predicts anticorrelated changes between the two FRET efficiencies, one between Cy3 and Cy5 (ECy3-Cy5) and the other between Cy3 and Cy7 (ECy3-Cy7) because when Cy3 on the dsDNA approaches Cy5, it should move away from Cy7 and vice versa.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the sliding model

claim: The time trace of ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7 exhibits anticorrelation between the two FRET efficiencies
source: Consistent with the sliding model, the time trace of ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7 exhibits anticorrelation between the two FRET efficiencies.
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3B

claim: The timescale of fluctuations from three-color assay (0.04 s) is similar to that measured using two-color assay
source: The timescale of fluctuations determined from the cross-correlation of the two FRET efficiencies (Txcorr-3color = 0.04 s) (Figure 3C) is similar to that measured using the two color assay (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown by comparing data from Figure 3C and Figure 2C

claim: Pearson's correlation coefficient for ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7 is -0.6
source: The scatter plot of ECy3-Cy5 vs ECy3-Cy7 and calculation of Pearson's correlation coefficient for the two FRET efficiencies (rpearson = −0.6) provide further support for a negative correlation between ECy3-Cy5 and ECy3-Cy7 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Two and three color FRET results cumulatively support the sliding model
source: Hence, cumulatively the two and three color FRET results support the sliding model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental results

claim: For 6 nt homology, the rate of departing HS1 or HS2 was threefold lower than that of leaving NH
source: The rate of departing HS1 or HS2 was threefold lower than that of leaving NH, showing that even 6 bp homology can significantly stabilize joint molecule formation (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is derived from HMM analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 4L

claim: Even 6 bp homology can significantly stabilize joint molecule formation
source: The rate of departing HS1 or HS2 was threefold lower than that of leaving NH, showing that even 6 bp homology can significantly stabilize joint molecule formation (Figure 4L).
evidence: This is inferred from the rate differences shown in Figure 4L

claim: The dissociation rate of dsDNA bound to HS1 was higher than that of dsDNA bound to HS2
source: Also, the dissociation rate of dsDNA bound to HS1 was higher than that of dsDNA bound to HS2 possibly because HS1 is located at the filament end where the terminal RecA monomer at the ssDNA–dsDNA junction binds with altered kinetics (Joo et al., 2006) as opposed to HS2 which is embedded within the RecA filament and benefits from complementary basepairing with the homology site and stabilizing interactions with neighboring RecA monomers.
evidence: This is observed in the data and explained by structural considerations

claim: Transitions occurred not only between neighboring sites but also involved NH->HS1 type transitions
source: Interestingly, transitions did not occur solely between neighboring sites (NH<->HS2 and HS1<->HS2 type transitions) but also involved transitions of the type NH->HS1 indicating that the RecA filament might overlook a region of homology during the sliding process.
evidence: This is observed in the transition density plots

claim: RecA filament might overlook a region of homology during the sliding process
source: Interestingly, transitions did not occur solely between neighboring sites (NH<->HS2 and HS1<->HS2 type transitions) but also involved transitions of the type NH->HS1 indicating that the RecA filament might overlook a region of homology during the sliding process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of NH->HS1 transitions

claim: The efficiency of homology recognition by RecA filament increases with the number of homologous nucleotides available for basepairing
source: Cumulatively, our data suggest that the efficiency of homology recognition by the RecA filament increases with the number of homologous nucleotides available for basepairing.
evidence: This is concluded from comparing recognition efficiencies for different homology lengths

claim: For 8 nt homology, dsDNA bound to HS1 and HS2 exhibited stable FRET states and transitions between them were rare
source: We could not perform a similar analysis for Lh = 8 nt since dsDNA bound to HS1 and HS2 positions in this case exhibited stable FRET states and transitions between them were rare (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: RecA filament sliding is a possible mechanism to assist homology search during strand exchange reaction
source: Our study establishes RecA filament sliding as a possible mechanism to assist homology search during strand exchange reaction.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study

claim: There has been no prior example of a multi-protein complex bound to DNA that can slide along a second DNA strand to locate a matching sequence
source: Until now, there has been no example of a multi-protein complex bound to DNA such as the RecA filament which is capable of sliding along a second DNA strand to locate a matching sequence of bases.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding in the context of existing literature

claim: The lifetime of heterologous synapses ranges from 0.5 to 10 s
source: Because the lifetime of heterologous synapses ranges from 0.5 to 10 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) (Mani et al., 2009; Forget and Kowalczykowski, 2012), we estimate that dsDNA would diffuse over a length of 60–300 bp during each encounter with a RecA filament prior to its dissociation.
evidence: This is based on experimental data and prior studies

claim: dsDNA would diffuse over a length of 60-300 bp during each encounter with RecA filament prior to dissociation
source: Because the lifetime of heterologous synapses ranges from 0.5 to 10 s (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) (Mani et al., 2009; Forget and Kowalczykowski, 2012), we estimate that dsDNA would diffuse over a length of 60–300 bp during each encounter with a RecA filament prior to its dissociation.
evidence: This is calculated from the diffusion coefficient and lifetime measurements

claim: Even for a recognition probability as low as 1%, sliding leads to a rate enhancement in homology search by approximately 200-fold
source: Though, we do not know the exact microscopic rate constants which determine the binding probability of the RecA filament to the target site (pbind), we can estimate that even for a recognition probability as low as approximately 1%, sliding leads to a rate enhancement in homology search by approximately 200-fold.
evidence: This is calculated from theoretical modeling shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: If no sliding is allowed and homology must be recognized via fortuitous 3D contact, homology recognition would be about two orders of magnitude slower
source: If no sliding is allowed and homology must be recognized via fortuitous 3D contact that aligns the dsDNA and filament in perfect registry, homology recognition would be about two orders of magnitude slower.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results

claim: 1D sliding combined with intersegmental transfer can dramatically accelerate homology search
source: Therefore, 1D sliding combined with intersegmental transfer proposed by Forget and Kowalcyzkowski (2012) can dramatically accelerate homology search.
evidence: This is concluded from the modeling and experimental results

claim: Changes in angle between dsDNA and RecA filament (off-axis motions) might affect the observed FRET changes
source: We cannot rule out the possibility that changes in angle between the dsDNA and the RecA filament (off-axis motions) might affect the observed FRET changes.
evidence: This is acknowledged as a limitation

claim: On-axis motion is the dominant source of FRET fluctuations
source: Incorporating such effects of off-axis motions into the model would increase the time scale of linear sliding but the effect will be small because control experiments such as the DNA length dependence (Figure 2C) showed that on-axis motion is the dominant source of FRET fluctuations.
evidence: This is inferred from control experiments shown in Figure 2C

claim: dsDNA flipping (180° change in orientation while remaining bound to RecA filament) does not occur
source: Although our experimental scheme cannot probe for small and dynamic off-axis motions between the RecA filament and dsDNA, we can at least rule out the extreme possibility of 'dsDNA flipping' in which case the dsDNA may undergo a 180° change in orientation while remaining bound to the RecA filament (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by control experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claim: A dsDNA that binds to RecA filament in the wrong orientation cannot establish the correct orientation without full dissociation and rebinding
source: Therefore, a dsDNA that binds to a RecA filament in the wrong orientation cannot establish the correct orientation required for homology recognition and basepairing without full dissociation and rebinding.
evidence: This is concluded from the flipping experiments

claim: As few as 6 nt of complementary base pairs are sufficient to act as the unit of homology recognition for RecA mediated homology search
source: Our results showed that as few as 6 nt of complementary base pairs are sufficient to act as the unit of homology recognition for RecA mediated homology search.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experiments with different homology lengths in Figure 4

claim: Recognition of a homology site is a stochastic process
source: It is noteworthy that recognition of a homology site is a stochastic process and the efficiency of homology recognition by the RecA filament depends on the length of homology which is encountered at a particular site.
evidence: This is inferred from the probabilistic nature of the transitions observed

claim: Adding a single nucleotide to the minimum recognition unit of 6 nt improves recognition efficiency by approximately 1.5-fold
source: Furthermore, we show that adding even a single nucleotide to the minimum recognition unit of 6 nt improves recognition efficiency by approximately 1.5-fold.
evidence: This is calculated from comparing 6 nt and 7 nt recognition efficiencies

claim: Proteins mediate target search reactions by a combination of 1D sliding and 3D diffusion based processes
source: Proteins mediate target search reactions by a combination of 1D sliding and 3D diffusion based processes (Gorman and Greene, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation

claim: 1D sliding during homology search could help RecA reorganize the initial synaptic complex in cis without full dissociation and rebinding
source: While intersegmental transfer serves to bring non-contiguous segments of dsDNA close to each other, 1D sliding during homology search could help RecA reorganize the initial synaptic complex in cis without the need for a RecA filament to fully dissociate and rebind to a nearby homology site located within a short distance (up to few hundred base pairs).
evidence: This is a functional interpretation of the sliding mechanism

claim: Sliding could serve as a mechanism to rapidly scan neighboring sequences for an optimal seed sequence
source: Given the ability of the RecA filament to slide between nearby homology sites (Figure 4), sliding could serve as a mechanism to rapidly scan neighboring sequences for the existence of an optimal seed sequence from which base pair propagation and heteroduplex extension reactions can proceed.
evidence: This is a functional interpretation based on the experimental results

claim: An earlier report demonstrated sliding of Rad51 oligomers without any clear functional role
source: An earlier report demonstrated sliding of Rad51 oligomers (not a Rad51 filament bound to ssDNA) without any clear functional role attributed to the observed sliding activity (Graneli et al., 2006).
evidence: This is prior knowledge supported by citation

claim: Sliding might also play a role in homology search mediated by Rad51
source: Because of significant structural and functional similarities between RecA and Rad51 (Conway et al., 2004), it is likely that sliding might also play a role in homology search mediated by Rad51.
evidence: This is speculated based on structural similarities

claim: RecA binding to ssDNA results in an average rise between successive nucleotides of 5.1 Å/bp
source: Since RecA binding to ssDNA results in an average rise between successive nucleotides of d = 5.1 Å/bp, L could be expressed by
evidence: This is a known structural parameter used in the modeling

claim: The persistence length of RecA-ssDNA is approximately 784 nm (approximately 2300 bp)
source: Since the persistence length of RecA-ssDNA was reported to be approximately 784 nm (approximately 2300 bp) (Hegner et al., 1999), the RecA-DNA filaments in our experiments can be simply treated as a rod in one dimension.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation
